entry: Ancient Greek goddess of hunting, the wilderness, wild animals, childbirth, and chastity. She was the daughter of Leto and [[Zeus]] and the twin sister of [[Apollo]]; her Roman equivalent is Diana. Artemis was one of the primary goddesses of childbirth and a patron of healing and disease, and was regarded as one of three major virgin goddesses. In myth, the hunter Actaeon, who saw her bathing, was transformed into a [[Deer|deer]] and devoured by his own dogs. In the [[Trojan War]], [[Agamemnon]] shot and killed her sacred deer, and Artemis halted the Greek fleet at Aulis. Her great temple at [[Ephesus]] was one of the [[Seven Wonders of the Ancient World]]. Her symbols included the bow, arrow, and quiver. She was later identified with Selene, the personification of the [[Moon]].

Italian [[Baroque]] painter. Gentileschi was born in [[Rome]], the eldest child of the painter Orazio Gentileschi, and trained in her father’s workshop. She was producing professional work by the age of 15, initially working in the style of [[Caravaggio]]. She became the first woman to be a member of the Accademia di Arte del Disegno in [[Florence]], and she had an international clientele. She worked as an expatriate painter at the court of [[Charles I of England]] and was known for depicting the female figure with naturalism and for her handling of color. Many of her paintings show women from myths, allegories, and the Bible, including *Judith Slaying Holofernes* and *Susanna and the Elders*. Her achievements were long overshadowed by the story of her rape at around 18 years old by Agostino Tassi and of her being tortured to give evidence at his trial. Scholars have since reexamined her life and art, and major exhibitions at the [[National Gallery]] in London have recognized her talents.

Blood vessel that carries blood away from the [[Heart|heart]] in the [[Circulatory system|systemic circulation]]. In humans and most other animals, arteries carry oxygenated blood to the body. The exceptions are the pulmonary arteries, which carry deoxygenated blood to the [[Lung|lungs]] for oxygenation, and the umbilical arteries, which carry deoxygenated blood to the [[Placenta|placenta]] in the fetal circulation. The artery wall has three layers, called tunics: the tunica intima, tunica media, and tunica externa (or tunica adventitia). The tunica media is made of smooth muscle cells, elastic tissue, and collagen fibers, and the elastic tissue allows the artery to bend. Arteries have higher [[Blood pressure|blood pressure]] than other parts of the circulatory system, and the pressure varies with the cardiac cycle, producing a [[Pulse|pulse]]. Arterioles have the greatest influence on local blood flow and overall blood pressure. Arteries contrast with [[Vein|veins]], which carry deoxygenated blood back toward the heart.

Ancient Indian [[Sanskrit]] treatise on statecraft, [[Politics|politics]], [[Economic policy|economic policy]], and [[Military strategy|military strategy]]. The text names Kautilya (Kauṭalya) and Vishnugupta as its compiler or redactor, but it is likely the work of several authors over centuries. According to Olivelle, its earlier treatises date from the 2nd century BCE to the 1st century CE, and the surviving manuscripts were most likely completed between the 1st and 3rd centuries CE. The text has 15 books, 150 chapters, and 180 topics. It covers government, law, court systems, ethics, markets and trade, diplomacy, war, and the duties of a king, and it incorporates [[Hindu philosophy|Hindu philosophy]]. It advises a king to build public projects, such as irrigation waterways, in areas devastated by famine, epidemic, or war. Its identification with [[Chanakya]], the legendary counselor of [[Chandragupta Maurya]], began during the Gupta reign and has been rejected by the main scholarly studies since 1965. The text was rediscovered in 1905 and first translated into English in 1915.

English science fiction writer, inventor, and undersea explorer. Clarke was a lifelong advocate of space travel, and in 1945 he proposed a [[Satellite|satellite]] communication system using [[Geostationary orbit|geostationary orbits]]. He wrote many books and essays for popular magazines, earning the nickname “Prophet of the Space Age,” and his science fiction won several Hugo and Nebula awards. During [[World War II|the Second World War]] he served in the Royal Air Force as a radar specialist. He co-wrote the screenplay for *2001: A Space Odyssey* (1968) with [[Stanley Kubrick]]. In 1956 he emigrated to Ceylon, where he discovered the underwater ruins of the ancient Koneswaram Temple in Trincomalee. He lived in [[Sri Lanka]] until his death, and in 1961 he received the Kalinga Prize, a [[UNESCO]] award for popularizing science.

English mathematician. He helped found the modern British school of [[Pure mathematics|pure mathematics]] and was a professor at Trinity College, [[Cambridge]], for 35 years, working mostly on [[Algebra|algebra]]. He postulated the Cayley–Hamilton theorem, that every square matrix is a root of its own characteristic polynomial, and verified it for matrices of order 2 and 3. He was the first to define an abstract [[Group (mathematics)|group]], a set with a binary operation satisfying certain laws, in contrast to [[Évariste Galois]]’s concept of permutation groups. Cayley tables, Cayley graphs, and Cayley’s theorem in group theory are named for him, as is Cayley’s formula in [[Combinatorics|combinatorics]]. After practicing law in London for fourteen years, during which he produced between two and three hundred papers, he became the first Sadleirian professor at Cambridge.

British writer and physician. He is best known for four novels and fifty-six short stories about the consulting detective [[Sherlock Holmes]] and his assistant Watson, which are milestones of [[Detective fiction|crime fiction]]. He studied medicine at the University of [[Edinburgh]] and served as a doctor and surgeon on two sea voyages before an unsuccessful medical practice in Portsmouth. His novel *The Lost World* (1912), featuring Professor Challenger, gave its name to a subgenre of speculative fiction. He was knighted by King [[Edward VII]] in the 1902 Coronation Honours. He twice stood unsuccessfully for Parliament, wrote in support of compulsory vaccination, and personally investigated two closed cases, both resulting in the exoneration of the accused men. Doyle became a spiritualist and publicly supported the Cottingley Fairies, later confirmed to be a hoax, which led to a public falling-out with [[Harry Houdini]].

American playwright and essayist. His plays include *All My Sons* (1947), *Death of a Salesman* (1949), *The Crucible* (1953), and *A View from the Bridge* (1955). *Death of a Salesman* won a Pulitzer Prize for Drama and is considered one of the best American plays of the 20th century. *The Crucible* drew on the [[Salem witch trials]] to address mass hysteria. The family lost almost everything in the [[Wall Street crash of 1929]]. After graduating, Miller joined the Federal Theatre Project, a [[New Deal]] agency, and he later held faculty posts at [[New York University]] and the University of New Hampshire. He testified before the House Un-American Activities Committee and married [[Marilyn Monroe]]. He also wrote the screenplay for *The Misfits* (1961).

French poet. Born in Charleville, he produced most of his literary output in his late adolescence and early adulthood, and his transgressive, surreal verse prefigured [[Surrealism|surrealism]]. He ran away to Paris during the [[Franco-Prussian War]]. He had a hectic, sometimes violent relationship with the poet Paul Verlaine that lasted nearly two years. His *A Season in Hell* is a precursor to [[Modernism|modernist]] literature, and his work contributed to [[Symbolism (movement)|symbolism]]. He stopped writing literature at about age 20, after assembling *Illuminations*. He then traveled on three continents as a merchant and explorer, working as a coffee trader in [[Aden]]. He died of [[Cancer|cancer]] after a leg [[Amputation|amputation]].

Polish and American pianist. Widely regarded as one of the greatest pianists of his day, he was acclaimed for his [[Classical music|classical]] interpretations, particularly of Chopin. He played in public for eight decades, with a repertoire including Beethoven, Brahms, Mozart, Schubert, Liszt, Tchaikovsky, Saint-Saëns, and Schumann. Born in [[Łódź]], in Congress Poland, which was then part of the [[Russian Empire]], he moved to [[Berlin]] at age ten to study. He gave his first performance with the Berlin Philharmonic in 1900, at age 13. In 1904 he moved to Paris, where he met [[Maurice Ravel]]. In 1912 he made his London debut and found a musical home in the salon of Paul and Muriel Draper, where he associated with [[Igor Stravinsky]] and [[Pablo Casals]]. During World War I he stayed in London, and in 1916 and 1917 he made his first tours of Spain and South America.

German philosopher and writer, known as the “Philosopher of Pessimism.” His main work, *The World as Will and Representation* (1818; expanded 1844), characterizes the phenomenal world as the manifestation of a blind and irrational noumenal will. Building on the transcendental idealism of [[Immanuel Kant]], he developed an atheistic, metaphysical, and ethical system that rejected the contemporaneous ideas of [[Idealism|German idealism]]. He was among the first Western philosophers to affirm significant tenets of [[Indian philosophy]], such as [[Asceticism|asceticism]], denial of the self, and the notion of the world as appearance. His work attracted little attention during his lifetime. His writing on aesthetics, morality, and psychology later influenced many thinkers and artists. He lived for much of his later life in [[Frankfurt]].

British Army officer and statesman. Born in [[Dublin]] into an Anglo-Irish family, he fought in India during the Fourth Anglo-Mysore War, winning at Seringapatam in 1799, and won a decisive victory over the Maratha Confederacy at the Battle of Assaye in 1803. He rose to prominence in the [[Peninsular War]] and was promoted to field marshal after the victory at Vitoria in 1813. Following Napoleon’s first exile in 1814, he was made Duke of Wellington and served as British ambassador to France. During the Hundred Days in 1815, his army and a Prussian army under Field Marshal Gebhard von Blücher defeated [[Napoleon]] at the [[Battle of Waterloo|Battle of Waterloo]]. A Tory, he served as prime minister from 1828 to 1830 and briefly in 1834, oversaw the Roman Catholic Relief Act 1829, and opposed the Reform Act 1832. He remained a leading figure in the [[House of Lords]] until 1846.

Variety of thistle (*Cynara cardunculus* var. *scolymus*) cultivated for its edible flower buds. The buds are eaten before the [[Flower|flowers]] bloom; the edible parts are the fleshy lower bracts and the base, known as the heart. The artichoke is a domesticated form of the wild cardoon, a perennial native to the Mediterranean region. The English word was borrowed in the sixteenth century from northern Italian *articiocco*, which derives from Arabic. In 2022 global production reached 1.58 million metric tons, led by Egypt (460,000 tons), Italy (378,000 tons), and Spain (200,000 tons). In the United States, production is concentrated in [[California]]. Fungal pathogens including *Verticillium dahliae* and *Rhizoctonia solani* affect the plant.

Hypothetical type of [[Artificial intelligence|artificial intelligence]] that matches or surpasses human capabilities across most or all cognitive tasks. Unlike artificial narrow intelligence, it could generalize knowledge, transfer skills between domains, and solve novel problems without task-specific reprogramming. Companies including OpenAI, [[Google]], and Meta have stated creating it as a goal. The concept is common in [[Science fiction|science fiction]]. Some experts argue that mitigating the risk of human extinction from it should be a global priority, while others consider it too remote to present such a risk.

Island constructed by humans rather than formed through natural processes. Although there is no clear legal definition, artificial islands were built as early as the [[Neolithic]] era. In modern times they are usually formed by [[Land reclamation|land reclamation]]. Al-Sayah Island in [[Bahrain]] is described as the world’s first permanent artificial island, created at least 1,200 years ago around a water spring. The Aztec city of [[Tenochtitlan]], predecessor of [[Mexico City]], stood on a natural island surrounded by artificial islands. Dejima, a contained center for European merchants, was built in the bay of [[Nagasaki]] during Japan’s [[Edo period]]. [[Ellis Island]] was a former islet greatly expanded by land reclamation. Dubai’s Palm Jumeirah extends 5 kilometers into the Persian Gulf. China’s artificial islands in the South China Sea have intensified territorial disputes.

Ranged weapons that launch munitions far beyond the range and power of infantry firearms. The first known [[Catapult|catapult]] was developed in Syracuse in 399 BC, and early artillery was designed to breach walls and fortifications during sieges. Until the introduction of [[Gunpowder|gunpowder]], artillery depended on mechanical energy; a 1st-century BC Roman catapult launching 6.55 kg (14.4 lb) stones achieved 16 kilojoules, compared with 240 kilojoules for a mid-19th-century 12-pounder gun. Since the introduction of gunpowder and cannon, the term has largely meant shell-firing guns, [[Howitzer|howitzers]], [[Mortar (weapon)|mortars]], and rocket artillery. Artillery caused the majority of combat deaths in the [[Napoleonic Wars]], [[World War I]], and [[World War II]]. In 1944, [[Joseph Stalin]] called artillery “the god of war.”

Order of placental mammals, typically ungulates that bear weight equally on two of their five toes. The name comes from Greek *ártios* (“even”) and *dáktylos* (“finger, toe”). Many artiodactyls digest plant cellulose in one or more stomach chambers rather than in the intestine. Molecular and fossil evidence places [[Cetacean|cetaceans]], such as whales, dolphins, and porpoises, within the group, most closely related to hippopotamuses. The roughly 270 land-based even-toed ungulate species include pigs, antelopes, [[Deer|deer]], camels, [[Cattle|cattle]], and hippopotamuses. The oldest fossils date to the early [[Eocene]], about 53 million years ago. Many artiodactyls are of great dietary, economic, and cultural importance to humans.

Person who creates [[Art|art]] or practices one of the arts. The most common usage refers to a practitioner of the visual arts, such as [[Painting|painting]] or drawing. The term is also used in entertainment for [[Actor|actors]], musicians, singers, and dancers, and is less commonly applied to [[Writer|writers]], for whom “author” is generally used. There is no agreed definition of art, so the question of who is an artist remains indeterminate. The word derives from Middle French *artiste*, from Latin *ars*, meaning skill. In ancient Greece, each of the nine [[Muses]] presided over a field of human creation, but none was associated with painting or [[Sculpture|sculpture]], whose makers were held in low regard and whose work was often done by slaves.

Discipline of gymnastics in which athletes perform short routines on different types of apparatus. World Gymnastics governs the sport and assigns the Code of Points used to score elite international competition. The gymnastic system was mentioned in writings by [[Homer]], [[Aristotle]], and [[Plato]], and it evolved in Bohemia and Germany at the beginning of the 19th century. Gymnastics was included in the 1896 [[Summer Olympic Games|Summer Olympics]], but women were not allowed to compete until 1928. Women’s and men’s branches have since developed different techniques and apparatus. [[Larisa Latynina]] won 18 Olympic medals for the Soviet Union, and [[Simone Biles]] won 11 Olympic medals as a U.S. gymnast.

International trend in the [[Decorative arts|decorative]] and fine arts that developed earliest and most fully in the [[British Isles]], then spread across the [[British Empire]] and to Europe and North America. It was a reaction against the perceived decline of design standards associated with machinery and factory production. Design reformers, including Henry Cole and Owen Jones, criticized the exhibits at the Great Exhibition of 1851 as excessively ornate. The term was first used in 1887 by T. J. Cobden-Sanderson, and the movement flourished between about 1880 and 1920. It drew on the ideas of Thomas Carlyle, John Ruskin, and William Morris. Some consider it the root of the Modern Style, while others regard it as opposed to [[Art Nouveau]], which it criticized for its use of industrial materials such as iron. In Japan, it emerged in the 1920s as the Mingei movement.

Italian conductor. Known for his intensity, perfectionism, and eidetic memory, he was at various times music director of La Scala in [[Milan]] and of the New York Philharmonic. He began conducting at 19 in [[Rio de Janeiro]], when he took the podium to lead *Aida* after the audience booed the substitute conductor, and he conducted 18 operas over the rest of that season. He was the first music director of the NBC Symphony Orchestra (1937–1954), and his radio and television broadcasts and many recordings made him a household name, especially in the United States. In 1931 he resigned from La Scala rather than conduct the Fascist anthem *Giovinezza*, and he opposed Fascism.

Island constituent country of the [[Kingdom of the Netherlands]] in the southern Caribbean Sea, 29 km north of the Venezuelan peninsula of Paraguaná. It became a constituent country in 1986. With an area of 179 sq km, Aruba is one of the [[ABC islands]] with [[Bonaire]] and [[Curaçao]]. Its climate is dry and arid. With a population of 108,880, it has Oranjestad as its capital.

State in northeast India, with Itanagar as its capital. It became a state in 1987. It borders [[Bhutan]] to the west and [[Myanmar]] to the east, and to the north it has a disputed border with the [[Tibet Autonomous Region]] of China, which claims nearly four-fifths of the state as Southern Tibet. The 2011 census recorded 1,383,727 residents, with 17 inhabitants per sq km, the lowest density of any Indian state.

Indian author and political activist. Her novel *The God of Small Things* (1997) won the [[Booker Prize]] for Fiction and became the biggest-selling book by a non-expatriate Indian author. She is involved in human rights and environmental causes. In 2024 she won the PEN Pinter Prize, sharing it with the imprisoned British-Egyptian writer and activist Alaa Abd El-Fattah, whom she named the “Writer of Courage.”

Indian mathematician-astronomer. He was a native of Kusumapura (Pataliputra), near present-day [[Patna]], in Bihar, and he is regarded as the first of the major mathematician-astronomers of the classical age. His surviving work, the *Āryabhaṭīya*, covers arithmetic, [[Algebra|algebra]], plane and spherical [[Trigonometry|trigonometry]], continued fractions, quadratic equations, and a table of sines. It approximated [[Pi|π]] as 3.1416 (expressed as 62,832/20,000). He proposed that the Earth is spherical and rotates daily on its axis, and he explained solar and lunar eclipses by the shadows of the Earth and the [[Moon]]. He is also reputed to have set up an observatory at the Sun temple in Taregana, Bihar. His lost *Arya-siddhanta* was referenced by later writers, including [[Brahmagupta]].
